prompt: What does storing a table column by column make cheaper? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of a query naming 3 columns of 40.

choices.text: Reading one whole row
choices.why: It visits every column's run.

choices.text: Reading a few columns of a wide table
choices.why: Yes. The other columns are not touched.

choices.text: Adding one row at a time
choices.why: That means rewriting the file.

choices.text: Compressing the data
choices.why: Yes. Values of one column look alike.

prompt: Order the parts of a Parquet file from largest to smallest.
hint: A page is the unit that is compressed.

prompt: Why does a Parquet reader open the footer before anything else?
hint: What does the footer record for every column chunk?

choices.text: The footer holds the first row group's data
choices.why: It holds metadata only.

choices.text: It contains the decryption key
choices.why: Nothing here is encrypted.

choices.text: The file is compressed backwards from the end
choices.why: Pages are compressed one by one.

choices.text: It says where each chunk is and what values it holds
choices.why: Right. From it the reader decides what to read.

prompt: In the silver layer's file, why did `kind` take 16 KiB and `ts` 532?
hint: How many different values does each have?

choices.text: Strings are stored more compactly than timestamps in every format
choices.why: `visitor_id` is a string and took 157 KiB.

choices.text: `ts` is compressed with a weaker codec than `kind`
choices.why: Both were Snappy.

choices.text: `kind` has four values; `ts` differs in every row
choices.why: Right. A dictionary shrinks the first and cannot help the second.

choices.text: `ts` is stored twice, once per row group
choices.why: That file had one row group.

prompt: Which changes took January from 33.0 MiB to 7.2? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three changes, all made when writing.

choices.text: Version 2 pages
Sorting the rows by book
choices.why: That made the files larger.

choices.text: zstd instead of Snappy
Timestamps as `TIMESTAMP_MICROS`

prompt: Why was the gzipped CSV smaller than Spark's default Parquet?
hint: Compare the codecs, not the formats.

choices.text: Parquet stores every value twice, once in the footer
choices.why: The footer holds sizes and ranges, not values.

choices.text: Snappy trades size for speed; gzip is stronger
choices.why: Right. Parquet with gzip was close to the CSV.

choices.text: A columnar file cannot be compressed
choices.why: It is compressed page by page.

choices.text: CSV files have no header row
choices.why: These have one, and it is tiny.

prompt: Why did the timestamps only shrink once they were written as `TIMESTAMP_MICROS` and with version 2 pages?
hint: Which types does delta binary packing accept?

choices.text: zstd only compresses integers
choices.why: A codec only sees bytes.

choices.text: Version 1 pages cannot hold timestamps
choices.why: The silver layer's v1 pages held them.

choices.text: `INT96` timestamps lose their time zone
choices.why: Size, not correctness, was the issue.

choices.text: Delta encoding needs integers, and comes with v2
choices.why: Right. `INT96` is not an integer type it accepts.

prompt: Match each encoding to what it stores.

pairs.right: The first value, then each difference from the one before
Each distinct value once, and a small number per row

right_distractors: The values sorted, with their row numbers

prompt: A column of 65,754 timestamps takes 164.3 KiB after delta encoding and before compression. About how many bits per row is that? (1 KiB = 8,192 bits)
Why could the silver layer skip no row group for `book_id >= 2900`?
hint: What range does each day's footer give for `book_id`?

choices.text: Parquet cannot skip row groups on an integer column
choices.why: The sorted copy skipped them on the same column.

choices.text: The filter was applied by a Python function
choices.why: It was a plain column comparison.

choices.text: Every row group ran from book 1 to 3000
choices.why: Right. No range ruled the filter out.

choices.text: The files were compressed with Snappy
choices.why: Statistics do not depend on the codec.

prompt: With the sorted copy, how many million rows did the scan hand on for the rare books? Round to a whole number.
The rows read fell 24 times, but the time only from 5.4 to 5.1 seconds. Why?
hint: What did both scans still have to do for every file?

choices.text: Both still opened 365 files and read their footers
choices.why: Right. Sorting does not touch that cost.

choices.text: Skipped row groups are read anyway and thrown away
choices.why: Skipped means not read.

choices.text: The cluster cached the silver layer in between
choices.why: Nothing was cached.

choices.text: The sorted copy was read without its statistics
choices.why: It used them to skip row groups.

prompt: In the sorted copy with fifteen row groups, why did `visitor_id` nearly triple in size?

choices.text: Sorting by book duplicated the visitors
choices.why: The rows are the same.

choices.text: Visitor ids lost their dictionary encoding entirely
choices.why: The footer still lists a dictionary.

choices.text: The codec was changed for that column
choices.why: Every column was Snappy.

choices.text: Each row group keeps its own dictionary
choices.why: Right. A visitor in ten row groups is spelled out ten times.

prompt: Which column should a table usually be sorted by within its partitions?

choices.text: The largest column on disk
choices.why: Sorting by it may shrink it, and help no query.

choices.text: The one most queries filter on
choices.why: Right, unless it is already the partition column.

choices.text: The first column of the schema
choices.why: Position means nothing to a reader.

choices.text: The one with the most distinct values
choices.why: That is about the data, not about the questions.

prompt: Where Parquet has row groups, ORC has ___.
hint: Like the bands on a flag.

prompt: A team's lake is read by Spark, DuckDB and a cloud warehouse, through lesson 11's table formats. Which file format fits?
hint: Which one is those tools' default?

choices.text: Avro
choices.why: Avro stores rows, not columns.

choices.text: ORC, because it came out smaller here
choices.why: The bytes rarely decide it; the rest of the system does.

choices.text: Parquet
choices.why: Right. It is their default and the table formats' default.

choices.text: Gzipped CSV
choices.why: CSV is for arriving, not for staying.

prompt: When does a bloom filter on a column pay off?
hint: What can it answer that minimum and maximum cannot?

choices.text: For range filters on a sorted column
choices.why: Minimum and maximum already serve those.

choices.text: For equality filters on a column whose ranges say nothing
choices.why: Right, such as a visitor id.

choices.text: For columns with four distinct values
choices.why: Every row group would hold them all.

choices.text: For every column, at no cost
choices.why: It costs space in every file.

prompt: Match each problem to the change in how the data is written.
hint: Each came from a section of this lesson.

pairs.left: Files twice the size of the gzipped CSV
A timestamp column that will not shrink
Every query filters on a column and skips nothing
pairs.right: Sort by that column within partitions

pairs.left: Equality lookups on a random id read every row group
pairs.right: A bloom filter on that column

prompt: A table is written once a night and read by fifty reports a day. Where should effort go?

choices.text: Nowhere, because the codec decides it all
choices.why: Codec, types, page format and sort order all mattered.

choices.text: Into each report, filtering after reading everything
choices.why: Fifty times the work the write could have saved.

choices.text: Into caching the raw CSV in memory
choices.why: Lesson 9: that saves only a read.

choices.text: Into the write, to make every read cheaper
choices.why: Right. It is paid once and saved fifty times.
